narrative:
The model estimates you have a 13% chance of failing your final year, which is low enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you will fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. While this is the same as the average for students who passed, the model sees the complete absence of any prior academic setbacks as unexpectedly increasing your risk this year. Second, although you have a clear desire to pursue higher education, the model interprets this ambition, in combination with your other choices, as not providing enough protective push toward success. Third, your low weekend alcohol consumption actually works in your favor and pulls the prediction back toward passing.

Taken together, the lack of any history of struggle appears to have been interpreted by the model as a warning sign that you may not be prepared for the final year’s demands, outweighing the positive effects of your educational goals and sensible weekend habits.

To improve, you should treat the remedial courses as an opportunity rather than a punishment. Focus on building steady study habits beyond your current pattern of less than two hours per week, since most students who pass dedicate noticeably more time. Use the extra support sessions to identify any hidden gaps early, and consider whether your family relationships or social life might be quietly limiting your focus. Small, consistent changes now can turn this 13% risk into a passing grade.
